summary: THREX is a web tool where you type a sky position and watch real SPHEREx images of it as a time-lapse to spot what moves, checked on a known asteroid (6 Hebe, 766 arcsec measured vs 765 predicted by JPL). An extra toolkit predicts how a hypothetical Planet X would move and whether SPHEREx could see it. It matters because SPHEREx re-maps the whole sky and moving objects are hard to spot by eye in so much data.
details:
THREX answers the challenge in two parts.

1) The viewer (front page of the Streamlit app). The user types an RA/Dec or picks one of the five challenge targets: Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855-0714, RW Aurigae and R Draconis. The app lists the real SPHEREx exposures that covered the position (IRSA SIA2 search), aligns small 5-arcmin cutouts on a north-up grid and plays them as a time-lapse with a frame slider. Every frame shows its UTC date, wavelength and exposure ID. Flagged pixels can be shown, the zodiacal-light model is removed, two frames can be subtracted, the SIMBAD catalogue position is marked, and the brightness stretch can be per frame or fixed. The app warns that every exposure samples a different wavelength, so brightness changes between frames are colour, not variability.

Cached data (so the app works offline): evenly spaced subsets of the exposures IRSA lists: Barnard's Star 68 of 358, Epsilon Indi B 69 of 458, WISE 0855-0714 69 of 258, RW Aurigae 66 of 335 and R Draconis 61 of 539 (2025-04 to 2026-10). Custom RA/Dec queries work only when IRSA's search answers.

Proof on a moving object: the known asteroid 6 Hebe (2025-12-01). JPL Horizons predicts its position in each frame; two groups of frames 13.2 hours apart show it at the predicted places: 766 arcsec measured vs 765 arcsec predicted. JPL sb_ident lists 6 Hebe in the field. Hebe saturates the detector, so only its positions are meaningful. It was already known: nothing was discovered.

What we do not see: the catalogue proper motions of the five targets amount to only about 1 to 2 pixels over the period covered, so none is visible by eye (we did not measure them). WISE 0855-0714 is extremely faint below about 1.6 micron (Luhman and Esplin 2016), so a faint source near its position at those wavelengths is most likely a background blend; we claim no detection. R Draconis is saturated in most short-wavelength frames and its variability was not analysed.

2) Extra pages: what would a hypothetical Planet X look like? Using the published best-fit orbit (Brown and Batygin 2021: about 380 AU, about 6.2 Earth masses) we compute how Planet X would move as seen from Earth and how bright it would be in reflected sunlight. For example, at 400 AU with a radius of 3 Earth radii and an albedo of 0.4 it would be AB 19.4 to 21.5 depending on the band, close to or below SPHEREx's sensitivity; over six months Earth's motion alone shifts it by about 1000 arcsec (about 160 pixels). Our orbit code agrees with JPL Horizons to 0.4 arcsec for Sedna and Eris. The orbit angles are demo values, and the radius, albedo and single-visit depth are assumptions. Planet X is hypothetical and no detection is claimed. Everything is labelled measured, computed or assumed.

Why it matters and what is new: SPHEREx maps the whole sky repeatedly, and moving objects such as asteroids, brown dwarfs or a possible Planet X are hard to spot by eye in so much data. THREX lets anyone look at one sky position across all of its real exposures, quickly, and connects that view to physics: Earth's motion shifts a distant object's apparent position between visits, and the extra pages turn this into a measurable signature and a brightness estimate for a hypothetical Planet X. The creative part is putting a time-lapse viewer, a check against JPL predictions on a real asteroid, and a feasibility estimate in one open tool.

Tools: Python, Astropy, astroquery, NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, Pillow and Streamlit, tested with pytest (38 tests); no special hardware is needed. To run it: pip install -r requirements.txt, then streamlit run app.py. Source code: https://github.com/kabilGa/threx-spaceapps

Code, documentation, charts and slides were created with SI assistance (Claude Code, Anthropic). Images and slides carry a visible SI label, and code, data and PDF metadata acknowledge it; see AI_USE.md in the repository.
